author: A Robot
objectives: Determine the steric number of a central atom from its Lewis structure.
Predict electron-domain geometries from steric numbers (2 to 6).
Distinguish between electron-domain geometry and molecular geometry.
Explain the effect of lone pairs on bond angles using repulsion concepts.
Correlate VSEPR predictions with real, observed molecular shapes.

modules.description: Learn the core repulsion principle and how to count electron domains from flat Lewis structures.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Identify electron repulsion as the driving force of molecular geometry
Count electron domains from a standard Lewis structure
instructions: Observe the central atom and listen to how electron repulsion determines 3D shapes.
Examine the Lewis structure panel to learn how to count electron domains.

components.text:
Lewis Structure of Water:
  H - O - H
  (plus 2 lone pairs on O)
  Total domains (Steric Number) = 4
VSEPR: Valence Shell Electron Pair Repulsion

clips.changeMeaning: Initial setup showing central oxygen atom and general introduction to the repulsion principle.
clips.narration: Welcome to the VSEPR Theory Lab. Valence Shell Electron Pair Repulsion theory is a powerful model that predicts the 3D shape of molecules based on a simple idea: electrons are negatively charged and repel each other. Thus, electron domains around a central atom arrange themselves to be as far apart as possible.

clips.changeMeaning: Lewis structure panel appears to guide the student on counting electron domains.
clips.narration: To predict a molecule's shape, we start with its flat Lewis structure. Here, we count electron domains around the central atom. Each single bond, double bond, triple bond, or lone pair counts as exactly one domain. For example, water has four total domains around oxygen: two single bonds and two lone pairs.

modules.description: Observe how 2, 3, and 4 electron domains repel each other to form stable 3D geometries.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Visualize physical repulsion of electron domains
Recall linear, trigonal planar, and tetrahedral arrangements and their ideal angles
instructions: Watch the electron lobes migrate to find their minimum-repulsion angles.

clips.changeMeaning: Two electron lobes appear close together to illustrate the start of the repulsive movement.
clips.narration: Let's look at how domains physically rearrange. Imagine two electron domains starting close to one another. Their negative charges instantly push them apart. Watch them migrate until they settle at the maximum possible distance.

clips.changeMeaning: The two domains migrate to opposite ends, showing a 180 degree linear layout.
clips.narration: They settle 180 degrees apart, producing a Linear electron-domain geometry. This configuration minimizes repulsion between the two domains.

clips.changeMeaning: A third domain lobe is introduced, causing all three to rearrange to 120 degrees trigonal planar.
clips.narration: Adding a third domain forces a new rearrangement. To keep all domains equally far apart, they spread out in a single plane, creating a Trigonal Planar geometry with bond angles of exactly 120 degrees.

clips.changeMeaning: A fourth domain lobe is introduced, forcing the molecule into a 3D tetrahedral structure.
clips.narration: When we add a fourth domain, the system is forced into three dimensions. It escapes the flat page to form a Tetrahedral geometry. The maximum separation angle is now 109.5 degrees.

modules.description: Explore the more complex geometries with steric numbers 5 and 6: trigonal bipyramidal and octahedral.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Distinguish axial and equatorial positions in trigonal bipyramidal systems
Identify octahedral symmetry and its universal 90-degree angles
instructions: Examine the positions of the axial and equatorial domains in the rotating structures.

components.text:
Electron-Domain Geometries:
  • 2 Domains: Linear (180°)
  • 3 Domains: Trigonal Planar (120°)
  • 4 Domains: Tetrahedral (109.5°)
  • 5 Domains: Trigonal Bipyramidal (90°/120°)
  • 6 Domains: Octahedral (90°)

clips.changeMeaning: 5 domains are shown, creating a Trigonal Bipyramidal arrangement with distinct axial and equatorial lobes.
clips.narration: Next, let's explore steric number five: Trigonal Bipyramidal. This geometry is unique because the positions are not all chemically equivalent. The two axial positions align vertically at 90 degrees to three equatorial positions that are spaced 120 degrees apart.

clips.changeMeaning: A 6th equatorial domain is added to form the octahedral structure.
clips.narration: With six electron domains, we achieve Octahedral geometry. Highly symmetrical, all six domains sit at 90-degree angles to their neighbors. They are fully equivalent, like six points on a perfect sphere.

clips.changeMeaning: A central summary catalog panel displays all five fundamental geometries.
clips.narration: Take a moment to review the five core electron-domain geometries. These layouts form the structural canvas for all covalent molecular shapes we will look at next.

modules.description: Discover how replacing bonding domains with lone pairs alters the visible molecular geometry while maintaining the tetrahedral base.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Distinguish electron-domain geometry from molecular geometry
Recognize the molecular shapes: tetrahedral, trigonal pyramidal, and bent
instructions: Observe how the underlying tetrahedral skeleton stays the same while the molecular shape changes.

components.text:
Methane (CH4)
  4 Electron Domains (Tetrahedral EDG)
  4 Bonding / 0 Lone Pairs
  Molecular Geometry: Tetrahedral

clips.changeMeaning: Displaying a molecule where all domains are bonding, showing that EDG and Molecular geometry match.
clips.narration: Now let's distinguish electron-domain geometry from molecular shape. If all domains are shared with outer atoms, the two geometries match. For methane, CH4, we have four bonding domains: both the electron-domain and molecular geometry are tetrahedral.

components.text:
Ammonia (NH3)
  4 Electron Domains (Tetrahedral EDG)
  3 Bonding / 1 Lone Pair
  Molecular Geometry: Trigonal Pyramidal

clips.changeMeaning: One bonding domain is replaced by a translucent yellow lone pair cloud to show ammonia.
clips.narration: In ammonia, NH3, one bonding pair is replaced by a lone pair. The underlying electron-domain geometry is still tetrahedral, but because we only 'see' atoms to define molecular shape, the molecule's geometry is now Trigonal Pyramidal.

components.text:
Water (H2O)
  4 Electron Domains (Tetrahedral EDG)
  2 Bonding / 2 Lone Pairs
  Molecular Geometry: Bent

clips.changeMeaning: A second bonding domain is replaced by a lone pair to show water's bent geometry.
clips.narration: For water, H2O, we replace a second bonding pair with a lone pair. Again, the four domains remain tetrahedral in layout, but the visual molecular geometry traced by the remaining three atoms is Bent.

modules.description: See why lone pairs occupy more space, squeezing bond angles down from the ideal 109.5°.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Explain why lone pairs exert greater repulsive force than bonding pairs
Compare experimental bond angles of CH4, NH3, and H2O
instructions: Compare the size of the translucent lone pairs and watch how they compress bonding angles.

components.text: Lone pair electrons are held by one nucleus: they spread out and repel bonding pairs more strongly.

clips.changeMeaning: Show methane, ammonia, and water side by side to contrast their structures and angles.
clips.narration: Why do lone pairs make a difference? Because lone pairs are attracted to only one nucleus (the central atom) rather than shared between two. Consequently, they spread out, occupying a larger volume of space and squeezing the nearby bonding pairs closer together.

clips.changeMeaning: Fade in comparisons of specific measured angles showing deviations from 109.5.
clips.narration: This spatial asymmetry explains experimental angles: while methane has perfect tetrahedral angles of 109.5 degrees, ammonia's single lone pair pushes the H-N-H bond angles down to 107 degrees. Water's two massive lone pairs squeeze the H-O-H angle down further, to 104.5 degrees.

modules.description: Examine real chemical substances in 3D representing different structural domains.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Identify 3D geometries of real-world chemical structures
Connect Lewis structures to physical 3D configurations
instructions: Observe how the 3D structures spin and examine their relative symmetry.

clips.changeMeaning: Showcase real molecules side-by-side representing different steric geometries.
clips.narration: Let's step into the physical gallery of real molecules. Here we have Carbon Dioxide, Boron Trifluoride, Sulfur Hexafluoride, and Xenon Tetrafluoride. Observe how closely physical geometry matches our VSEPR models.

clips.changeMeaning: Highlight individual configurations, turning on simple rotation for deeper spatial visualization.
clips.narration: Carbon Dioxide is perfectly linear. Boron Trifluoride is completely planar. Highly symmetric geometries like Sulfur Hexafluoride are perfectly octahedral. Xenon Tetrafluoride features two axial lone pairs that we don't see, resulting in a physical square planar shape.

modules.description: Interactive test: Drag domains into position to satisfy the minimum repulsion rule.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Construct the spatial configuration of the trigonal planar geometry
Verify structural angles for electron domains
instructions: Grab and drag the floating domains to construct the correct minimum-repulsion shape.

components.scriptDescription: Monitors the child electron lobes. When they form angles within 15 degrees of a perfect 120 degree configuration, it disables dragging and plays a success sound.

components.text: Drag the 3 domains to minimize repulsion!

clips.changeMeaning: Interactive setup: students must drag domains around the central atom.
clips.narration: Now it's your turn. Below you will see three floating electron domains. Try grabbing and dragging them around the central atom. Your goal is to arrange them to satisfy the minimum-repulsion rule.

clips.changeMeaning: Simulate a snap-into-place configuration for the solved trigonal planar geometry.
clips.narration: Excellent work. When domains are configured near 120 degrees apart, they stabilize. This minimizes the repulsion forces across all domains perfectly.

modules.description: Look at a Lewis structure and pick the correct molecular geometry from multiple 3D choices.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Deduce steric number and molecular geometry of unfamiliar compounds
Select 3D shape matching the molecular geometry
instructions: Look at the Lewis structure of SF4. Click on the 3D model option (A, B, or C) that represents its true shape.

components.text:
Sulfur Tetrafluoride (SF4)
  Lewis Structure:
     F      F
      \    /
       :S:
      /    \
     F      F
  (4 single bonds, 1 lone pair)
Pick an option on the right.

clips.changeMeaning: A Lewis structure appears for Sulfur Tetrafluoride (SF4), and students must pick the 3D molecular structure option.
clips.narration: Look at the Lewis structure for Sulfur Tetrafluoride on the left. Sulfur has four bonds and one lone pair, yielding five total domains. Click the sphere that matches the correct physical molecular geometry.

components.text: Correct! SF4 has 5 domains (4 bonding, 1 lone pair). The lone pair occupies an equatorial site, leaving a Seesaw molecular shape.

clips.changeMeaning: Feedback confirms option B (Seesaw) is correct, disabling incorrect options.
clips.narration: That's correct! In a 5-domain system, lone pairs occupy the roomier equatorial sites to minimize 90-degree repulsions. Removing one equatorial domain leaves us with the Seesaw molecular geometry.

modules.description: Review the fundamental rules of VSEPR theory and molecular shapes.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Review connection between steric numbers and geometries
instructions: Read through the lab summary and review the concepts before exiting.

components.text:
VSEPR Lab Summary:
  1. Repulsion pushes electron domains as far apart as possible.
  2. Steric Number (Bonds + Lone Pairs) sets Electron-Domain Geometry.
  3. Lone Pairs are larger and squeeze remaining bond angles.
  4. Molecular Geometry traces only the physical atoms.
  5. Geometries range from Linear (2 domains) to Octahedral (6 domains).

clips.changeMeaning: A final summary screen lists the five core areas covered.
clips.narration: Congratulations, you've completed the VSEPR lab! We have covered how steric numbers define electron-domain layouts, how lone pairs occupy extra space and squeeze remaining angles, and how to predict physical molecular geometries from flat Lewis structures. Keep these tools in mind as you explore the shapes of chemistry!
